story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Cody, I have 847 YouTube playlists, and always hated that YouTube failed to provide basic playlist management tools. Ctrl+F was never convenient and breaks past 200 playlists. So I built & shipped my first Chrome extension. It replaces the Save dialog with a native-feeling searchable one that fetches all your playlists (and whether the current video is saved there) directly from YouTube's InnerTube API. It works robustly across every current save surface (watch page, home feed, search results, Shorts via right-click or Alt+S).

This version is faster and more stable than my original attempt. In 1.0 I read and wrote YouTube's DOM directly. It felt like the efficient approach, but makes for constant UI regressions as YouTube changes, so I can't recommend it. In 2.0 the UI lives outside YouTube's app tree in a closed shadow root, and the data comes from YouTube's internal InnerTube JSON API. The trigger it uses is a small hook wrapping the page's fetch, i.e. when YouTube's client requests the add-to-playlist panel.

Privacy: As private as possible given it's a YouTube extension. The extension only talks to youtube.com, doesn't ship any third-party code, and stores nothing about your playlists, just two display preferences: sort order, and the privacy new playlists are created with. AGPL-3.0.

Install: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/efgbkmnooapcpdpgmih... Source: https://github.com/codyhxyz/playlist-search-extension Site: https://playlist.codyh.xyz/

Bonus: Technically you can replicate the filter-bar functionality with a dev console script, which I've linked here: (https://gist.github.com/codyhxyz/00001e74d238ae5911ccfc8f8d4...). For obvious reasons, I prefer a dedicated extension.

Happy to answer anything about my approach including the InnerTube API or about the shadow-root. Always looking to improve the extension's architecture.

title.value: Show HN: You Can Just Filter YouTube Playlists in the 'Save to Playlist' Dialog

Spent a whole week's worth of tokens on industry event research validating event dates, finding prices, filtering junk events, de-duping, and generally cleaning up the data. May it be useful to other founders trying to sell.

story_text.value:
After the recent eMudhra CA incident, I wondered why my system trusts over 150 root signing authorities, most of which I don't need?

I decided to scratch my own itch and make a tool to block the long tail of unwanted CA certificates.

distrust is a policy-based tool that aims to simplify the management of the mess of root stores: browsers (NSS, Chrome Root Store), OpenSSL/GnuTLS consumers (curl, wget, Python, Go), Java, and the standalone PEM bundles that apps ship (certifi, conda, botocore).

It ships with an example policy that blocks all CAs except the top 30. I've tested and this seems fine for my normal browsing and usage.

There did not appear to be existing tools to do this, probably because there is so much variance across operating system platforms, distros, and programming languages. distrust is therefore shamelessly vibe-coded to deal with all these edge cases.

https://github.com/hyperreality/distrust

title.value: Show HN: distrust, a Go CLI tool for blocking unwanted CA certificates

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Faithful. I built dánwò, an open-source (Apache-2.0) end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps, written in TypeScript.

The problem: a UI test can click "Pay", see "Payment successful" and pass, while the card was charged twice, the webhook was handled twice, or the receipt email never went out. With coding agents writing more of our code, that gap between "the screen looks right" and "the right things happened" is where I kept finding bugs.

How it works:

- Tests drive the app like a user, with locators or plain-English agent steps. An agent step calls a model once; danwo records the actions and replays them on later runs with no model calls, so CI doesn't need an API key.

- Your app runs behind an egress proxy. Calls to Stripe, Clerk, Resend, Slack, Google and about 20 other providers are answered by local emulators at the real hostnames, so there are no sandbox keys and no code changes. For Node apps a preload routes the calls; Bun honours HTTPS_PROXY.

- An invariant is a check that runs after the test and compares two sides: what the provider says happened (charges, emails, messages) and what your app stored. For example, credits granted must equal paid checkouts times 500.

- `danwo matrix` replays a test once per fault it could meet: a 500 or 429 from a provider, a declined card, a duplicate, late, forged or replayed webhook, a double-submit, a database commit whose reply is lost, Postgres unreachable for a few seconds. The invariant judges every run, so you see exactly which failure your app mishandles.

- Every run leaves a flight record: video, each step, every provider call, webhook delivery and database statement, with secrets redacted.

It runs in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and on the Android emulator and iOS Simulator. It ships an MCP server and a skill, so coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can write and run tests and fix what fails.

Limitations, honestly: the emulators are only as good as their fidelity to the real APIs. Each one has a suite that runs against the real provider to catch drift, but they won't cover every edge of Stripe's API. Backend routing is built for Node and Bun today. Mobile tests need macOS or Linux. It's early (v0.1.2).

The name is Yorùbá: "dán an wò" means "try it and see".

Quickstart: npx @danwo/cli init (docs: https://danwo.dev/docs/quickstart)

I'd love feedback, especially on faults you've been bitten by that aren't in the matrix yet.

title.value: Show HN: Dánwò – Open-source E2E testing with emulators and fault injection

story_text.value:
Hi HN. Sillage (French for the wake a boat leaves behind) is a small browser game with no goal.

You're a blob: hold the mouse or a finger down to swim toward it, and fast currents carry you into the next world. Creatures and backgrounds inspiration come from Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur.

On the creative process:

I've wanted to make something like this for years, since reading Jenova Chen's thesis on flow in games (https://www.jenovachen.com/flowingames/missionstatement.htm) - whose studio later created games like Flower or Journey - and Daniel Shiffman's The Nature of Code (https://natureofcode.com), which I had backed on kickstarter.

In 2012 I made this octopus: https://github.com/dhovart/octopus, and later I spent some evenings on a small game system in rescript: https://github.com/dhovart/rescript-game

All of this was before LLMs, when small idea still took me hours and most of them stayed half built.

I like shaders, especially fragment shaders - these are things that I am very slow to get right and to have full control on. You look up effects, try to implement them, tweak numbers, look at the result, change them again, and hours have past already. I spent lots and lots of time on shadertoy.

Now all of this is getting incredibly cheap to implement because of LLMs. That's part infuriating to have a robot code better than you and also very satisfying to experiment with things that are in your mind in a very short iterative cycle.

I felt like I was half art director, half manager of a talented studio crew - and I'm very pleased with the result.

title.value: Show HN: Sillage, a small contemplative game drawn after Haeckel's plates

story_text.value:
Hey everyone,

Inspired by Herdr, I've built an agent multiplexer that I've been using as my daily driver for a few weeks now.

I think I improved on the concept in a few ways, focusing on the ergonomics I always wished I had:

I show you what the agents are up to, along with a running feed of their activity. There's also a simple shortcut (F1) to go to the next unread agent.

I use multiple accounts, so I've added unified launcher for Codex/Claude Code/Pi. Theres some careful ergonomics there: fast search and resume over sessions, inline usage tracking etc.

Many small quality of life improvements to the terminal experience: - Links can be copied with a click, so no need to drag-select over many lines - cmd+v just pastes images (even on SSH) - images have a thumbnail preview. - Built-in CPU/Memory/GPU usage tracking, broken down by workspace

I assume you have access to cheap inference (Luna/Haiku/etc). It just reuses the agents to organize things for you: what is this http link? what is this worktree about? what is each agent doing? It's small but it made my environment feel more cozy.

On a personal note, I've been on a frustrating sick leave for a while now. I created Corgi to challenge myself, and see if I can go back. The answer is more mixed than I had hoped, but I am happy with the result and thankful for the experience.

I hope you like it! a few friends & myself have been using it for a few weeks and it's been pretty nice. There's still a lot to improve and some rough edges, so feedback would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you :)

title.value: Show HN: Corgi, a helpful {agent, terminal} multiplexer

story_text.value:
I use shared markdown files to collaborate with agents. Their biggest complaint was that, when content changed, they needed to either re-read the full file or write code to find the difference.

So I made mdt. It's light - one binary, one sqlite file - and lets your agent track the changes to a shared file, so that it only reads the diff.

Ping me if I can make it better.

story_text.value:
Information pollution affects all of us. When we are served a random mix of important news, half-truths and “For You” posts from strangers in the same feed, our ability to make sense of the world are diminished.

Over time, it wears us down.

Robin is an open source Twitter/X client for iOS and Android. It restores a clean, chronological set of posts (only from people you follow.) You can hide posts using keywords (e.g. noisy politicians' names.) It also lets you fact-check claims quickly by long-pressing on the post.

Our goal is simple – Lower the amount of distractions and the unwanted stress caused by hot takes and replies from random people we don’t know nor care about.

Launch post: https://evergreen-labs.org/blog/introducing-robin

iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/robin-non-algorithmic-x/id6817...

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.evergreenl...

Public Repo: https://github.com/billylo1/Robin

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Instant Search is the first accurate local AI file search that uses the latest embedding models from Perplexity to find the exact file (and page) with the content you’re looking for with a 95% hit rate.

Search never worked properly, especially with local files. Now, you can find the right image, document, or Obsidian file in seconds. Looking for your driver’s license? Just type “driver’s license”. Looking for a particular note? Just explain the context.

Why not Finder/Spotlight?

Spotlight is just a keyword search. It doesn’t understand file content. Instant finds the exact file you’re describing in under a second.

Why not RAG?

Traditional RAG models give you a single embedding vector per entire body of text. That means either you have a vector that’s not detailed enough to give you an accurate semantic representation, or it’s too precise and doesn’t contain enough surrounding context. Instant circumvents these problems by relying on a bidirectional late-interaction embedding model that works flawlessly.

How much space does indexing need? An average library of content needs less than 1GB of disk space.

Check it out, share with friends, and let me know your feedback! It's free.
